lines.text: an integrated substrate edits the floor that's already there
lines.note: the floor is the automaton, and a floor must be crossable: a BFS refills whatever the pattern killed between spawn and teleporter, so the first rule the learner meets has already been overruled by the need to carry them.

lines.text: Connect each new cell to a neighbor and a network appears — ancestry creates structure
Symmetry imposed on local rules transforms noise into ornament — the rug designs itself
3D structure growth simulation
lines.note: the argument is that 256 is small enough to walk: eight bits enumerate every rule, and a room cannot hold 256 walls, so one 26-neighbour 3D automaton stands where the enumeration should be and completeness stays a claim.

lines.text: Stack time as space and a flat automaton becomes architecture
the mandala is not emergent. A fragment is computed and the rest is copied — and this
A bridge built by a rule — you walk on computation
lines.note: you walk on computation, and no three-cell rule knows it owes you a floor: rule 110 computes and fills 49.7% of the deck, rule 250 fills 87.5% and computes nothing — the crossing costs the argument.

lines.text: Growth toward a goal, with noise, is enough to produce every vascular pattern in nature
lines.note: the vascular claim needs somewhere to grow toward: eight attractors are placed before the first tip moves, so the growth stays local only because the global information was smuggled in ahead of it as goals nobody grew.

lines.text: Slime mold network generation
Simple rules, applied everywhere simultaneously, produce complexity no one designed
Six neighbors instead of eight — the shape of the neighborhood reshapes the world
A tree is what remains when you remove everything that isn't tree
When every row speaks a different rule language
Architecture that reacts to presence is architecture that is alive
lines.note: reacting to presence is not a local rule: every tick the bridge asks the whole scene tree for a node in group "player" and decays within two cells of the answer — the reach that matters is a lookup, not a neighbourhood.

lines.text: The same rules on a sphere produce forms no flat grid ever could
lines.note: "the same rules" needs the same neighbourhood everywhere, and a sphere has none to give: this one is a 64-by-32 lat-long mesh, crowded at the poles and thin at the equator, so the automaton's world is the mesher's.

lines.text: Rule 30/110 with gravity effects
Five copies of yourself, arranged just so, and you contain yourself forever
lines.note: authorship over the rule is the payoff and no procedure comes with it: nothing runs from a wanted behaviour back to a rule number, so writing a rule here is searching 256 of them and looking.

lines.text: An 8-bit number is a universe — Rule 110 proves that three neighbors and one bit can compute …

pearls.edge: two rule systems meet and neither can say who won: Conway keeps no score, so the chamber imports one — a perturbation that outlives a few ticks counts as a contribution, and the clock does the judging.

lines.text: Screen display that renders live cellular-automata patterns
There are two ways to die — freeze into one thing
lines.note: narrowness can only be shown by leaving the band, and nothing here can leave: lambda is a constant 0.5 with no slider in the map, so the edge of chaos is walked from inside it and the two deaths stay named, not met.

lines.text: Two probabilities and a grid of neighbors — this is how pandemics actually work
Fog is a cellular automaton — local density rules produce clouds no one shaped
